options.description: C# on .NET, published as a self-contained executable for each platform (win-x64 and linux-x64), optionally compiled ahead of time with Native AOT. The .NET runtime is bundled into the output, so the target machine needs no installed runtime. The team copies the Windows and Linux builds to the network share. Coordinators run the .exe directly, and the Linux shell scripts call the Linux binary. CSV, GeoJSON and REST handling use .NET libraries or NuGet packages compiled into the build.

Python, frozen into a standalone bundle for each platform with a packaging tool such as PyInstaller or Nuitka, or shipped with the Windows embeddable Python distribution next to the scripts. The interpreter and all dependencies (CSV, GeoJSON, HTTP libraries) are copied into the bundle folder on the share, so no system Python is needed. Coordinators run a launcher executable or batch file. The Linux agents run a separate Linux-built bundle from the shell scripts.

Go, compiled into one static native binary per platform by cross-compiling from a single machine (GOOS=windows and GOOS=linux). The binary has no runtime or library dependencies and is copied to the network share as one file per platform. The standard library covers CSV, JSON parsing and HTTP calls to the ArcGIS REST API. Coordinators and the Linux shell scripts run the binary directly with command-line arguments.

C# on .NET (LTS release), compiled ahead of time with Native AOT into one native executable per platform (win-x64 and linux-x64). Each executable has no runtime dependency and is copied to the network share. CSV parsing, GeoJSON reading (System.Text.Json), validation rules, and REST calls to the feature service (HttpClient, token auth, applyEdits in batches) are written in C#. Reflection-heavy libraries are avoided or replaced with source-generated equivalents so that AOT trimming works.

C# on .NET (LTS release), published self-contained with the JIT runtime, using ReadyToRun precompilation and single-file bundling, one build per platform. The .NET runtime ships inside the bundle, so nothing is installed on the laptop or the build agents. The code uses the normal .NET library ecosystem without AOT restrictions (for example, a NuGet CSV library and reflection-based JSON). The share holds a Windows bundle and a Linux bundle built from the same source.

Python 3, packaged with a freezing tool (for example PyInstaller or the embeddable Python distribution plus a launcher) into a self-contained folder per platform that includes the interpreter and libraries. The share holds a Windows folder and a Linux folder, each run through a single entry executable. The code uses the standard csv and json modules or small libraries for parsing, a validation module, and the requests library for the ArcGIS REST calls. Each platform's build runs on that platform.

Go, compiled into one statically linked executable per platform by cross-compiling from a single machine (GOOS=windows and GOOS=linux). The executables need no runtime and are copied to the share. The standard library covers CSV parsing, JSON decoding of GeoJSON, HTTP calls to the feature service REST endpoints, and log file writing. Validation rules are written as Go functions or loaded from a config file. The team would learn Go for this tool.

C# on .NET 8 or later, compiled ahead of time (Native AOT) into one self-contained executable per platform (win-x64, linux-x64). The executable contains its own runtime, so the laptops and build agents need nothing installed. CSV is parsed with a library such as CsvHelper, GeoJSON with System.Text.Json, and uploads use HttpClient against the feature service applyEdits endpoint. The team copies both binaries and a rules file to the network share.

Python 3, with the Windows embeddable Python distribution (a zip with the interpreter and standard library) placed in a folder on the share next to the tool's scripts and its vendored packages. A small .cmd launcher runs the embedded interpreter. The Linux agents use the same scripts with a pinned Python on the agent or a portable build. Parsing uses the csv and json standard modules; uploads use requests or urllib to call the REST API.

Go, compiled into one statically linked executable for each platform from one codebase through cross-compilation (GOOS=windows and GOOS=linux). The binary has no runtime dependency. Parsing uses encoding/csv and encoding/json from the standard library, and uploads use net/http to post batches to the feature service. The team learns Go for this tool, and the share holds the two binaries plus a configuration file.

PowerShell scripts, with no compile step. On Windows the tool runs on PowerShell 7 extracted from the official portable zip into a folder on the share, and the Linux agents use the same portable PowerShell build. Import-Csv and ConvertFrom-Json read the inputs, validation rules are script functions or inline C# loaded with Add-Type, and Invoke-RestMethod calls the feature service. A .cmd wrapper starts the script for coordinators.

C# on a .NET LTS release, compiled ahead of time with Native AOT into one native executable per platform (win-x64, linux-x64) with no runtime dependency. Both binaries and a rules file go on the network share. CSV parsing, GeoJSON reading with System.Text.Json source generation, validation rules, and HttpClient calls to the feature service applyEdits endpoint (token auth, batched) are written in C#. Reflection-heavy libraries are avoided or replaced so that AOT trimming works.

C# on a .NET LTS release, published self-contained with the JIT runtime, ReadyToRun precompilation and single-file bundling, one build per platform from the same source. The .NET runtime ships inside each bundle, so laptops and build agents need nothing installed. The code uses the normal .NET library ecosystem without AOT restrictions, for example a NuGet CSV library such as CsvHelper and reflection-based JSON. The share holds a Windows bundle and a Linux bundle.

Python 3, frozen with a packaging tool such as PyInstaller or Nuitka into a self-contained folder per platform that holds the interpreter and all libraries. Each platform's bundle is built on that platform. The share holds a Windows folder and a Linux folder, each started through one entry executable. Code uses the csv and json standard modules or small libraries, a validation module, and requests for the ArcGIS REST calls.

Python 3 with the Windows embeddable distribution (a zip with interpreter and standard library) placed on the share next to the tool's scripts and vendored packages, started by a small .cmd launcher. The Linux agents run the same scripts on a pinned Python on the agent or a portable build. Parsing uses the csv and json standard modules; uploads use requests or urllib against the REST API. No freezing step is used.

Go, cross-compiled from one machine (GOOS=windows, GOOS=linux) into one statically linked executable per platform with no runtime dependency. The share holds the two binaries plus a configuration file. The standard library covers parsing (encoding/csv, encoding/json), HTTP batch posts to the feature service (net/http), and log writing. Validation rules are Go functions or loaded from config. The team learns Go for this tool.

PowerShell scripts with no compile step, run on PowerShell 7 extracted from the official portable zip into a folder on the share, with the same portable build on the Linux agents. Import-Csv and ConvertFrom-Json read the inputs, validation rules are script functions or inline C# loaded with Add-Type, and Invoke-RestMethod calls the feature service. A .cmd wrapper starts the script for coordinators.

result.baseline: Change nothing: build no new tool, and keep the current way coordinators and the nightly jobs validate and load inspection data into the feature service.

claims.text: No runtime or installer is needed. Native AOT yields a self-contained native executable, so locked-down laptops just run a file copied from the share. This meets the no-admin, no-install constraint directly.

Native AOT avoids JIT and runtime startup cost, so a 10-row file should finish well under 1 second on the laptops. Typical AOT hello-world starts in tens of milliseconds, a wide margin. No measurement was made here.

All 4 developers write C# daily and know HttpClient, System.Text.Json and async. Zero language ramp-up means faster delivery and lower bug risk. New hires from the ArcGIS Pro add-in pool already know it, supporting the one-month-fix goal.

One language and one codebase produce identical behavior on Windows and Linux. Two RIDs (win-x64, linux-x64) come from the same source, and the two Linux agents already exist to build the Linux binary.

500 nightly invocations of one file each are cheap with AOT startup, so process-launch overhead is negligible against the 2-hour window. Run time will be dominated by network round-trips to applyEdits, not the language.

System.Text.Json source generation and HttpClient are supported by Native AOT. The feature service work (CSV, GeoJSON, token auth, batched applyEdits) needs only the BCL, so few third-party dependencies are needed and AOT trimming is feasible.

Choose .NET 10 LTS, not .NET 8, since .NET 8 support ends around Nov 2026. Retargeting to the next LTS later is a routine one-line change that the team already practices with Pro SDK upgrades. No paid licenses are needed.

Strong typing, a debugger and IDE tooling the team already owns make a new hire's first bug fix practical. Rules in an external rules file let coordinators or developers change validation without recompiling.

weaknesses: Native AOT cannot cross-compile across operating systems, so each binary must be built on its own OS. It also restricts reflection and dynamic features. Any dependency that is not AOT-safe forces a rewrite, and AOT warnings add maintenance friction for new hires. Not verified.

Unsigned native executables run from a network share may be blocked or slowed by SmartScreen, AppLocker, antivirus scanning or Mark-of-the-Web policies on locked-down laptops. The under-1-second goal and no-help use are unverified on the real fleet, and code signing may be needed.

claims.text: Doing nothing has zero build cost and zero delivery risk. The team keeps its time for ArcGIS Pro add-in work, and no new code needs five years of maintenance.

The brief does not say the current process fails. If coordinators already load data and nightly jobs already finish in 2 hours, the success criteria are already met. A new tool must beat that, not just meet it.

The hard constraints (no install, under 1 second for 10 rows, same on Windows and Linux, self-contained files on a share) all cost effort for self-contained C# publishing. The baseline already runs inside these limits.
Staff turnover is normal. Existing tooling that people already know has a known learning cost. A new bespoke tool adds one more system a new hire must learn within the first month.
Rewrites of working internal tools often overrun. A 4-person team with no prior production use of this tool type is exposed to schedule risk, and the baseline carries none.

Choosing Option F does not close any door. Language choice can be revisited later with real data on failure rates, run times and coordinator help requests. Waiting loses little if the baseline is adequate.

weaknesses: I do not know what the current process is or how well it works. If it needs coordinator help, misses the nightly window, or cannot be maintained by new hires, the whole case fails.
I ran no research or tests. All claims are reasoned. The brief implies a new tool is wanted, which suggests the baseline has real problems that I cannot rule out.

claims.text: The official PowerShell 7 ZIP package is documented for side-loading: unzip anywhere and run pwsh.exe from there. No MSI or admin is mentioned, so it fits the no-installer, no-admin constraint on paper.

Execution policy is not enforced on Linux. It is Unrestricted there and behaves like Bypass. On Windows, a per-session `pwsh.exe -ExecutionPolicy` switch in the .cmd wrapper sets policy without admin, unless Group Policy overrides it.

Windows execution policy is documented as defense in depth, not a security boundary. A -ExecutionPolicy session switch in the .cmd wrapper therefore works in the common case where Group Policy does not set the policy.

Zero compile step and no build pipeline: scripts are plain text edited in place. A new hire can read and patch a script without a toolchain. This is the best case for the first-month-bug-fix criterion, though untyped code can offset it.

The team's C# skills carry over. Add-Type can hold validation logic as C#, and PowerShell 7 runs on .NET, so developers can call familiar BCL types such as HttpClient and System.Text.Json. Cmdlets cover CSV, JSON and REST.

Throughput probably fits the 2-hour window. 500 sequential files, each with a process start of about 0.3-0.6s plus parsing up to 50k rows, is likely well under 2 hours. The network round-trips to the feature service dominate in any language.

The portable ZIP is a single versioned folder on the share, shared by Windows and Linux with separate zips. There is nothing to install, and an upgrade means swapping the folder. This keeps the deployment simple.

The ZIP method means the team can pin an exact PowerShell version and avoid drift. The docs note a downloaded ZIP may need Unblock-File, which is a one-time step by the publisher rather than by coordinators.

weaknesses: The sub-1-second start on a locked-down laptop is unmeasured. pwsh startup from a network share, endpoint scanning (Defender or EDR) and Add-Type Roslyn compilation can each push a 10-row run past the limit. Add-Type compile cost is a real risk for inline C# rules.

Locked-down laptops may enforce Group Policy execution policy or AppLocker/WDAC. These can block an unsigned pwsh.exe or scripts run from a UNC share. Zone checks may also treat UNC paths as untrusted. Group Policy overrides the -ExecutionPolicy switch, so the plan could fail outright. Also, PowerShell has no static typing, which weakens 5-year maintainability and refactoring safety compared with C#.

claims.text: Single-file publish supports self-contained apps and combines with ReadyToRun. It is OS-specific, so one build per platform (win-x64, linux-x64) from one source matches Option M's two-bundle share layout.
Self-contained deployment carries the runtime inside the bundle, so locked-down laptops and build agents need no runtime or package manager, which satisfies the no-install, no-admin constraint.
ReadyToRun cuts JIT work at startup and on first use of code. The docs say apps with large amounts of code benefit most. That helps cold start but does not prove the 10-row under-1-second target.
The ReadyToRun compiler cross-compiles from a Windows x64 or Linux x64 SDK to both Windows and Linux x64 targets, so CI can build both bundles from one source tree and one build agent.

Skipping AOT and trimming allows reflection-based JSON and NuGet libraries like CsvHelper without trim or AOT warnings. This avoids the main source of the AOT option's maintenance risk. Applies to code the team writes.

All 4 developers write C# daily, and C# is the most common language in ArcGIS shops. A new hire from the GIS team can fix bugs in the first month with familiar tools, debugger and conventions, and no new language to learn.

Even-numbered .NET releases are LTS with 3 years of support. .NET 10 is supported to Nov 14, 2028, short of the 5-year maintenance horizon, but moving to the next LTS is a retarget plus rebuild, not a rewrite.

Per-file run time for 50,000 rows is dominated by HTTP uploads to the feature service, not language speed. 500 files per night in 2 hours leaves 14 seconds per file, which JIT-compiled .NET with ReadyToRun should meet unless startup is slow.

weaknesses: Startup under 1 second for a 10-row file on locked-down Windows laptops is unmeasured. Self-contained single-file bundles are large and may extract native libraries to a temp folder, as the docs describe. Antivirus scanning of a network-share executable could blow the budget, and the code-heavy ReadyToRun benefit is unproven.

The bundle is large (runtime plus framework, ReadyToRun roughly 2-3x assembly size), and 500 nightly launches each pay process startup. The .NET 10 LTS ends Nov 2028, so a retarget is needed within the 5-year window. Winning depends on the other options being worse, which this case cannot show.

claims.text: Go cross-compiles from one machine via GOOS/GOARCH. windows/amd64 and linux/amd64 are both supported targets, so one build host makes both binaries.

Go output is a single self-contained executable by default. The share holds two binaries plus a config file. Coordinators need no runtime or package manager, and deployment is a file copy with no admin rights.
Native compiled code has no VM or JIT warmup. A 10-row file should finish well under 1 second on a laptop, and 500 nightly invocations avoid per-process runtime startup costs. Not measured here.

A 50,000-row file with batched HTTP posts is I/O-bound on the feature service. Go's net/http and goroutines allow bounded concurrent batches, so the 2-hour nightly window is unlikely to be limited by language speed.

Effective Go says gofmt standardizes formatting and conventions make code easier for other Go programmers to read and maintain. This helps new hires and turnover. The page is from 2009 and not actively updated.
Errors are plain values checked explicitly, and success code runs straight down the page. That control flow is easy for a new hire to trace when fixing a bug in the first month.

The standard library covers CSV, JSON (including GeoJSON via encoding/json), HTTP, and logging. Few third-party dependencies means a small supply-chain surface over a 5-year maintenance life. Not checked against ArcGIS auth flows.
All 4 developers know C#, whose syntax and static typing are close to Go's. The learning cost is mainly idioms such as errors and goroutines, and a small CLI tool is a bounded first Go project.

weaknesses: Nobody on the team has shipped Go. Learning a new language plus its idioms is a real ramp-up risk. The hiring pool for Go in a GIS shop is thin, and a C# option would reuse existing skill, so this undercuts the turnover and first-month-fix goals.

Go has no mature ArcGIS or GIS-specific SDK. Token auth, geometry handling, projection and GeoJSON edge cases would be hand-written against the REST API, whereas C# has the ArcGIS Runtime and Pro SDK ecosystem. I did not research this, and the performance claims are untested.

claims.text: The Windows embeddable zip is official CPython, extracted to a folder and launched by running python.exe or a batch file. No installer, no admin rights, and no registry entries are needed. This fits the share-copy and locked-down laptop constraints.

The embeddable distribution is documented as almost fully isolated from system environment variables, registry and installed packages. A pinned interpreter on the share therefore behaves the same on every laptop. This supports coordinators running it without help.

Vendoring is the documented route: pip is not included or supported in the embeddable package, and the docs say third-party packages should ship alongside Python. A ._pth file can add a vendored folder. This design matches the docs, though it is manual.

Python's csv and json standard modules cover CSV and GeoJSON, and 50,000 rows is small. urllib alone can call the ArcGIS REST API with no third-party package. The dependency surface can be near zero, so the pinned zip stays simple to maintain.

A reported benchmark shows import requests at about 150 ms against about 64 ms for urllib.request. Using urllib, or a lazy import of requests, leaves room in the 1-second budget for a 10-row file. This is anecdotal and not measured on the target hardware.

All 4 developers know C#, and one knows Python well. Python's syntax and standard library are readable to C# developers. A new hire can fix a bug in a plain-text script by editing it in place with no build step, which supports the one-month goal.

Python behaves the same on Windows and Linux for csv, json and HTTP. One script tree serves both, and the Linux agents can use a pinned system Python or a portable build. No per-OS build matrix is needed. Python startup of tens of ms makes 500 invocations a night trivial.

No freezing step means no PyInstaller-style bundler, no antivirus false-positive risk from a self-extracting exe, and no rebuild pipeline. A fix is a file copy to the share. This lowers operational burden over 5 years of staff turnover.

weaknesses: Network-share performance is unverified. Python startup cost scales with file stat calls, which are slow over SMB. The sub-1-second requirement on laptops reading the interpreter and vendored packages from the share is unproven. The only evidence found was anecdotal, and the mitigation of copying to local temp adds complexity.

The team has no production Python experience beyond one person. Maintaining the pinned interpreter, ._pth setup, vendored packages and the security patch cycle for 5 years falls on C# developers. Python has no compile-time type checks, and the Linux agent interpreter policy is unspecified. A one-person bus factor on the Python knowledge is a real risk.

claims.text: PyInstaller bundles the Python interpreter and modules, so end users need no Python or packages. This directly satisfies the locked-down laptop constraint, with no installer or admin rights.

Default onedir mode produces a folder with one executable and all dependencies. A folder copied to a network share meets the 'files copied, no installer' constraint and avoids onefile's temp extraction.
Onefile decompresses to a temp _MEI folder at every launch and starts slower; onedir skips this. Choosing onedir protects the 1-second 10-row target and 500 nightly invocations.

PyInstaller output is specific to OS, Python version and word size, so one build per platform is required. This matches Option G's design of a Windows folder and a Linux folder built natively on two build agents.
PyInstaller supports Windows 8+ and GNU/Linux, needing only ldd and binutils on the build host. The build agents are Linux and can run it in CI, so both target platforms are officially covered.

All 4 developers know C# but one knows Python well. Python's csv/json modules and requests are small and readable, so a new hire can plausibly fix a bug in a month. This is the team's main hiring-pool advantage over C#.
50,000 rows of CSV/GeoJSON validation and batched REST uploads are I/O-bound on the network. Interpreter speed is unlikely to threaten the 2-hour window, even at 500 files per night.

Python bundles run unchanged logic on Windows and Linux with the same csv, json, and requests code. This gives one codebase and one test suite across platforms, with no per-OS conditional code beyond path handling.

weaknesses: Only one developer knows Python, and the other three write C# daily. Maintainability across 5 years of turnover rests on one person's expertise, while C# self-contained publishing would reuse everyone's existing skills and ArcGIS tooling.

Frozen Python bundles risk slow interpreter startup (about 0.3-1s or more with requests and its imports on locked-down laptops) and antivirus false positives or flagging of unsigned executables on network shares. I found no source confirming either point, so the 1-second constraint is unverified.
failedTests: WebFetch of https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/when-things-go-wrong.html returned no information on Python version support, Linux glibc compatibility, or Windows antivirus false positives. I could not verify these risks or mitigations with the budget used, so they are unresolved.
The requirements page also lacked glibc and Python-version guidance. No source confirms that a Linux bundle built on one agent runs on the other agents or on different distros.
No measurement of 10-row startup time was made; the rules forbid running tests.

challenges.text: H-C4 says one source gives both binaries and that the existing Linux agents build the Linux one. Native AOT cannot cross-compile between operating systems, and H-W1 concedes this. The win-x64 binary therefore needs a Windows build host with the C++ toolchain, and the Linux agents cannot make it. This is a second build environment the 4-person team must set up and keep for 5 years, and H-C4 does not count it.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft Native AOT deployment docs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/) list as a prerequisite on Windows: 'Visual Studio 2022, including the Desktop development with C++ workload'. The same docs say: 'Native AOT apps are platform and architecture specific' and 'Cross-compilation is not supported' between operating systems, apart from architecture cross-targeting with the right toolchain.

challenges.text: M-C2 says a self-contained bundle needs nothing installed on the laptops and build agents. A self-contained .NET app on Linux still depends on OS libraries it does not bundle, such as OpenSSL for HTTPS to the feature service and ICU for globalization. If either is missing, the app fails to start or throws on the first HTTPS call, unless InvariantGlobalization is set. The claim 'no runtime or package manager' therefore does not cover the Linux agents' own library state.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft .NET on Linux dependency docs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/install/linux) say that .NET, including self-contained apps, needs the distro's libicu and OpenSSL packages. The globalization docs say that without ICU an app fails at startup unless 'System.Globalization.Invariant' is set to true.

challenges.text: J-C8 says there is no antivirus or false-positive risk and that a fix is only a copy to the share. Running scripts and a python.exe from a UNC path on locked-down Windows is subject to Windows zone checks and to AppLocker or WDAC script rules. These apply to the .cmd launcher and to python.exe loaded from the share, so the risk J-C8 removes is replaced by a different policy risk. The claim also does not address J-W1, which says startup from SMB is unverified.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft AppLocker documentation (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/application-security/application-control/app-control-for-business/applocker/applocker-overview) says AppLocker rules cover executables, scripts (.bat, .cmd, .ps1, .vbs, .js) and DLLs by path, publisher or hash, so a .cmd launcher and a python.exe run from a network share can be blocked by policy. J-C1 also gives no source for how the embeddable python.exe behaves under such rules.

challenges.text: Choosing onedir avoids the onefile temp extraction, but it does not protect the 1-second target on its own. A onedir bundle is a folder of many files (interpreter DLL, extension modules, a PYZ archive, the requests dependency tree) that a coordinator would run from the network share. Per-file open and stat latency over SMB then applies at every launch, and 500 nightly launches repeat it. The claim cites only a comparison between onefile and onedir and gives no startup figure for a share-hosted onedir folder.
challenges.evidence: The cited PyInstaller operating-mode page (https://pyinstaller.org/en/stable/operating-mode.html) describes the default one-folder bundle as an executable plus a folder of dependencies, and describes onefile only as slower because it unpacks to a temp folder. It contains no startup measurement and no network-share guidance. The same case's G-W2 says 'I found no source confirming either point, so the 1-second constraint is unverified', and its failed-tests list says no startup time was measured. The 80 confidence is not supported by what was gathered.

challenges.text: The claim says one script tree behaves the same on Windows and Linux. The option's own design says Windows uses the embeddable zip on the share and Linux uses 'a pinned Python on the agent or a portable build'. That is a different interpreter source on each platform, and the claim does not pin down the Linux one. Vendored packages with compiled extensions also cannot be shared between a Windows and a Linux tree. The cited Portable-Python link is a repository home page and does not show a build that matches the Windows embeddable zip version.
challenges.evidence: J-C7 cites https://github.com/Portable-Python/portable-python, a project README with no statement about version parity with the Windows embeddable zip. J-W2 in the same case says 'the Linux agent interpreter policy is unspecified'. The Python docs page cited for Windows (https://docs.python.org/3/using/windows.html) says third-party packages must be shipped alongside the embeddable distribution, so any package with a compiled extension needs separate Windows and Linux copies. 'Same behavior on both platforms' is therefore not established at the stated 68 confidence.

challenges.text: The claim says C#'s syntax and static typing are close to Go's, so the cost to learn it is mainly idioms. The gap is larger than that. Go has no exceptions, no classes or inheritance, no LINQ-style collection operators, and no async/await. Error handling, concurrency and interface satisfaction all work differently. P-C6 in the same case relies on error values being checked explicitly, which shows that the control flow the C# team knows does not carry over. A 62 confidence treats an unmeasured ramp-up as small.
challenges.evidence: The Go FAQ states the design choice: 'We believe that coupling exceptions to a control structure, as in the try-catch-finally idiom, results in convoluted code' (https://go.dev/doc/faq#exceptions). The cited Effective Go page (https://go.dev/doc/effective_go) says Go uses goroutines and channels for concurrency and plain error values for failures. P-W1 in the same case says nobody has shipped Go and the learning is 'a real ramp-up risk'.

challenges.text: The claim says a -ExecutionPolicy switch in the .cmd wrapper works in the common case. The cited about_execution_policies page says a policy set by Group Policy takes precedence over a session-level setting, and the brief says the laptops are locked down. Locked-down fleets are the setting where MachinePolicy or UserPolicy is most likely to be set. Calling the common case 'Group Policy does not set the policy' assumes the opposite of the brief. Nothing in the claim shows that the target fleet leaves the policy unset.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft Learn, about_Execution_Policies (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_execution_policies?view=powershell-7.4) lists the scopes in order of precedence: MachinePolicy and UserPolicy come first, and the Process scope set by the -ExecutionPolicy parameter comes after them. N-W2 in the same case concedes 'Group Policy overrides the -ExecutionPolicy switch, so the plan could fail outright.' The 65 confidence is higher than that admission supports.

challenges.text: M-C4 says a Windows x64 or Linux x64 SDK can build both the Windows and Linux bundles, so one build agent can produce both. The cited table does not support that. A Linux x64 SDK cannot target Windows. Only a Windows x64 SDK can target both. The team's nightly build agents are Linux, so the 'one build agent, one source tree' claim fails unless a Windows build host is added. The Windows laptop bundle is the one that matters most for the 1-second constraint. This also weakens M-C1's 'one build per platform' layout, because the Windows build would need Windows infrastructure.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft Learn, ReadyToRun deployment overview (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/ready-to-run), section 'Cross platform/architecture restrictions', table for .NET 6 and later. Row: 'Linux X64 | Linux (X64, Arm32, Arm64), macOS (X64, Arm64)'. Windows is not listed. Row: 'Windows X64 | Windows (X86, X64, Arm64), Linux (X64, Arm32, Arm64), macOS (X64, Arm64)'. I fetched the page during this round.

challenges.text: J-C7 claims 'Python startup of tens of ms makes 500 invocations a night trivial' and that one script tree behaves the same on both platforms. Option J's own claims conflict with this. J-C5 reports 'import requests' at about 150 ms, and J-W1 says startup cost scales with file stat calls over SMB. J-C7 also leaves the Linux interpreter as 'a pinned system Python or a portable build', so the Linux runtime is not fixed. Its cited source is the Portable-Python project page, not a CPython release. That page does not show parity with the Windows embeddable zip, and it gives no startup measurement. The 'same on Windows and Linux' constraint therefore rests on an unspecified Linux interpreter, and the startup figure is an assumption.
challenges.evidence: Quoted from Option J's own text. J-C5: 'import requests at about 150 ms against about 64 ms for urllib.request'. J-W1: 'Python startup cost scales with file stat calls, which are slow over SMB'. J-W2: 'the Linux agent interpreter policy is unspecified'. J-C7 cites https://github.com/Portable-Python/portable-python, which is a third-party portable-build project. I made no measurement.

challenges.text: A rules file that coordinators or developers can change without recompiling does not fit an AOT-compiled binary that avoids dynamic features. The rules would need a custom rule format and a hand-written interpreter that the team must maintain for 5 years. Rules cannot be loaded as C# code at runtime.
challenges.evidence: Microsoft Native AOT documentation (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/) lists the limitations: 'No dynamic loading, for example Assembly.LoadFile' and 'No runtime code generation, for example System.Reflection.Emit'. H-W1 itself says AOT 'restricts reflection and dynamic features'.

challenges.text: H-C4 says one source tree and two RIDs give identical behavior, and that the existing Linux agents build the Linux binary. That conflicts with H-W1, where the case says each binary must be built on its own OS. The Windows binary therefore needs a Windows build host with the C++ toolchain, and that host is not in the brief. Nothing in the brief says a Windows build agent exists.
challenges.evidence: H-W1 in the same case: 'Native AOT cannot cross-compile across operating systems, so each binary must be built on its own OS.' The brief names only 2 Linux build agents. Microsoft's Native AOT prerequisites (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/deploying/native-aot/) require the Visual Studio C++ desktop workload on Windows.

challenges.text: The claim that unchanged csv, json and requests logic behaves the same on both platforms is overstated. Python's open() uses the locale encoding by default, which is a Windows ANSI code page on Windows and UTF-8 on Linux. CSV files exported from Windows tools therefore decode differently on the two platforms unless the code sets encoding everywhere. requests also verifies TLS against the certifi bundle, not the Windows certificate store. An ArcGIS Enterprise server with an internal CA would fail verification until the CA is bundled and managed.
challenges.evidence: Python docs for open() (https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open): 'The default encoding is platform dependent (whatever locale.getpreferredencoding() returns)'. Requests docs (https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#ca-certificates): 'Requests uses certificates from the package certifi.'

challenges.text: J-C7 says Python startup is tens of ms and 500 invocations are trivial. J-W1 says startup on the share is unproven because stat calls over SMB are slow. The claim also leaves the Linux interpreter policy open (J-W2), and its only citation is a Portable-Python repository that says nothing about startup time. The claim has no supporting measurement.
challenges.evidence: J-W1 in the same case: 'Python startup cost scales with file stat calls, which are slow over SMB. The sub-1-second requirement ... is unproven.' J-W2: 'the Linux agent interpreter policy is unspecified.' The cited link (https://github.com/Portable-Python/portable-python) is a build project, not a benchmark.

challenges.text: The 150 ms versus 64 ms import figures come from a 2017 python-dev mailing-list post, and they were run on hardware and a Python version unrelated to the target fleet. The post does not cover the vendored-package layout or the network share, where J-W1 says the cost is larger. The figures cannot support a conclusion that a 10-row run fits under 1 second.
challenges.evidence: The cited URL (https://mail.python.org/pipermail/python-dev/2017-October/149797.html) is dated October 2017. J-C5 itself says 'anecdotal and not measured on the target hardware'.

challenges.text: Go's syntax is not close to C#'s in the ways that matter for a first project. Go has no exceptions, classes or inheritance, uses explicit if err != nil handling, and its interface and package model differ from C#'s. The claim also contradicts P-W1, which says nobody has shipped Go and that the ramp-up is a real risk. P-C6 praises Go for error handling that differs from the C# exception model.

challenges.text: The claim that encoding/json covers GeoJSON and ArcGIS needs is unchecked, as the claim itself admits. GeoJSON geometry is polymorphic: the 'coordinates' array is nested to a different depth for Point, LineString and Polygon. Decoding it needs custom UnmarshalJSON code. applyEdits expects Esri JSON geometry, which is a different schema from GeoJSON, so a converter must be written by hand. P-W2 confirms this is hand-written.
challenges.evidence: RFC 7946 section 3.1 defines geometry coordinates with a different nesting for each type. The ArcGIS REST applyEdits documentation (https://developers.arcgis.com/rest/services-reference/enterprise/apply-edits-feature-service-layer/) takes features in Esri JSON form. P-C7 text: 'Not checked against ArcGIS auth flows.'

The 'works the same on Linux' constraint depends on the agent images, which are not specified.

challenges.text: The 14-second figure is arithmetic only. 7200 s / 500 files = 14.4 s per file. challenges.evidence: Calculation from the brief: 2 h = 7200 s; 7200/500 = 14.4 s per file; 50,000 rows / 14.4 s = about 3,472 rows per second. No source or measurement of applyEdits throughput is given in the case.

N at least specifies a tool that validates rows and writes a log. F gives no information about how the current process validates, retries, or records rejected rows (F-W1, F-W2). Its claim that the criteria are already met was ruled false (R9, R20, R29). So F gives me no assurance on correct uploads or rejection logs.
